journalArticles.title: Collective Action in the Sanctuary Movement: Polycentric Protection of Central American Asylum Seekers
journalArticles.authors: with Nathan Goodman and Karla Segovia
journalArticles.abstract: In the 1980s and early 1990s, civil wars contributed to significant waves of migration from Central American countries such as El Salvador and Guatemala. The United States federal government, specifically the Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS), systematically denied Central American immigrants' asylum claims and deported them back to war zones. In response, over 70,000 American citizens defied United States immigration laws in order to shelter Central American immigrants, transport them across the country, and provide them with sanctuary. This Sanctuary movement was largely led by people of faith, but it involved coordination across a wide variety of religious denominations. The size and heterogeneity of the movement, combined with the fact that their goals largely constituted a public good from the standpoint of supporters, presents a puzzle. How did participants in the Sanctuary movement successfully engage in collective action without succumbing to free riding and other social dilemmas? To answer this question, we analyze the polycentric networks and nested governance arrangements within the Sanctuary movement.

journalArticles.title: Fractured Families: The Unintended Consequences of Immigration Enforcement for Families
journalArticles.authors: with Nathan Goodman and Karla Segovia
journalArticles.abstract: Family integrity is an emergent result of individuals' attempts to coordinate plans on residence, caregiving, and economic support over time. U.S. immigration enforcement policies produce both intended and unintended consequences for the family, often undermining the stability of family units that are essential to society. Policies that separate children from parents at the border or detain and deport individual family members illustrate the direct use of the state to intentionally separate families. However, there are also unintended consequences of immigration policy that are of equal significance. Restrictions on circular migration have transformed temporary labor migration into long-term, often undocumented, settlement, forcing migrants to choose between financial support and physical presence with their family. Heightened border security has increased the danger of crossings, leading to ambiguous loss when migrants disappear in the desert, leaving family members in prolonged states of grief and uncertainty, disrupting short-and long-term plans. This paper argues that the consequences of U.S. immigration policy, whether intended or unintended, extend beyond the individual family unit and into the broader fabric of societies both domestically and internationally.

workingPapers.title: The Convergence Effect: AI and the Political Economy of State Capacities
workingPapers.authors: with Christopher Coyne and Abigail Hall Blanco
workingPapers.abstract: What is the effect of the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) on government operations and constitutional rules? The purpose of this paper is to explore the answer to this question through the lens of public choice and constitutional political economy. We explore the spread of generalpurpose technologies (GPTs) across government and how this spread enhances the state's coercive capabilities. To do so, we develop a theory of the "convergence effect" of GPTs. We apply this framework to Artificial Intelligence (AI) as an illustration. In doing so, we show how expansions in the scale and scope of government and the erosion of constraints on government may occur endogenously, without crises or other exogenous changes.
